newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka banks see better second half results.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka banks see better second half results.

text.p: Sri Lankan financial institutions and banks, which have seen mixed results in the first quarter of 1997 mainly due to shrinking margins, should see an improvement in profits in the second half, analysts said on Tuesday.

"Though profits of the banks were hit by eroding spreads in the first quarter, we expect strong credit calls due to lower rates to lead to aggressive lending in the second half of the year," said Channa Kurukulasuriya, head of research at brokerage Lanka Securities.

First quarter profits of Commercial Bank rose 16.6 perent to 97.96 million rupees, Hatton National Bank 5.8 percent to 107.97 and Sampath Bank 25 percent to 75.20. Results of Seylan Bank are yet to be released.
One of Sri Lanka's main development finance institutions -- National Development Bank said first quarter profits had fallen 10.4 percent to 149.88 million rupees.
The other, Development Finance Corporation, has yet to announce its first quarter result but analysts said its profits might also be lower.

Interest rates came under pressure when money supply improved after the Central Bank cut reserve ratio of commercial banks by three percent and allowed exporters foreign currency borrowings earlier in the year.
The benchmark 12-month treasury bill rate was at 12.74 percent on Monday, compared to a 1996 average of 16.6 percent.
The central bank also asked commercial banks to cut lending rates by between one and 1.5 percent.
"Big corporates now borrow working capital requirements at about 16 percent, down from around 18," said a foreign bank dealer. "Bigger cuts are sometimes affected on a case-by-case basis."
Sampath Bank, which showed the sharpest rise in first quarter profits, attributed the gains to fast responses to exporters' needs.
"We were nimble and moved fast to get the funding to meet needs of exporters who were moving away from rupee borrowings," Kumar Abayanayaka, chief executive of Sampath Bank told Reuters.
He said the bank expects to see substantial loan growth in the second half "as re-investment in business becomes more attractive at current rates."

"Sampath Bank also has the advantage of having low-cost funds unlike Hatton National, Seylan and Commercial which are locked into rigid deposit schemes," said Savanthi Arthenayake, financial sector analyst at brokerage Jardine Fleming.
Improved money supply and treasury bonds, which were launched recently by the government, have also hit banks with such deposit schemes, analysts said.

"With two and four-year treasury bonds yielding 12.96 percent and 12.25, banks with deposit schemes where they have to pay an average of about 14 to 15 percent, will have to readjust," Arthenayake said.
The government began issuing two-year treasury bonds in March this year and followed it up with four-year bonds last week.
Analsyts, however, say treasury bonds augur well for the medium to long-term development of financial institutions.
"Though treasury bonds could have a negative impact in the short-term, they will help the banks to develop a healthy mix of short and long-term lending," said Kurukulasuriya of Lanka Securities.
